payload.prompt: Which statements describe programmatic resource creation?

options.text: It uses code or scripts to create resources
options.rationale: Programmatic resource creation means using code or scripts. This is different from clicking through the Azure portal.
Scripts can repeat the same setup across environments. That makes deployments faster and more consistent.

options.text: It can reduce manual setup errors
options.rationale: Automation reduces repeated manual clicking. Fewer manual steps can reduce setup errors.

options.text: It requires clicking through portal screens
options.error_type: confuses programmatic creation with Azure portal management
options.rationale: Clicking through portal screens is manual Azure portal use. Programmatic creation uses code or scripts instead.
options.better_fit: Choose portal screens when you want visual Azure management.

feedback.intrinsic: A team trying to repeat setup could still make avoidable manual mistakes.
feedback.instructional: Programmatic creation means code or scripts. Portal screens are a visual management path, not the automated path.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Programmatic creation uses scripts or code for repeatable setup.

payload.prompt: Which statements describe Microsoft Entra ID and role-based access control, or RBAC?

options.text: Entra ID controls who can access AI resources
options.rationale: Microsoft Entra ID helps ensure only the right people and services can access resources. It is part of Azure access protection.

options.text: RBAC limits access based on roles
options.rationale: RBAC means role-based access control. It limits access by assigned roles.

options.text: RBAC can limit access to model deployments
options.rationale: RBAC can limit access to model deployments, resources, and data. That matches its role-based permission purpose.

options.text: RBAC stores API keys for runtime use
options.error_type: confuses role access with Key Vault secret storage
options.rationale: RBAC controls access by role. Azure Key Vault stores secrets such as API keys.
options.better_fit: Choose Key Vault when sensitive values need protected storage.

feedback.intrinsic: The team may set roles but still leave API keys without protected storage.
feedback.instructional: RBAC decides who can access resources. Key Vault protects sensitive values such as API keys.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Entra ID and RBAC are about identity and role-based access.

payload.prompt: Which statements describe Azure security and networking for AI applications?

options.text: Security includes identity and access control
options.rationale: Azure security includes built-in identity and access control. These capabilities help ensure only approved people and services can reach protected resources.
Azure networking helps resources connect reliably, privately, and efficiently. This matters for cloud and hybrid AI application environments.

options.text: Security can include threat detection and monitoring
options.rationale: Threat detection and monitoring are part of Azure security capabilities. They help teams identify risks and watch application health.

options.text: Networking means deleting stored app data
options.error_type: confuses networking with storage removal
options.rationale: Networking connects resources and supports secure communication. It does not mean deleting application data from storage.
options.better_fit: Choose storage management concepts when discussing saving, retrieving, retaining, or deleting application data.

feedback.intrinsic: A team might treat a connectivity and protection need like a data cleanup task.
feedback.instructional: Security and networking protect access and connections. Storage concepts handle persistent application data.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Security and networking cover access protection, private connectivity, monitoring, and threat detection.

payload.prompt: Which statements explain Azure storage for AI applications?

options.text: Storage saves and retrieves data for later use
options.rationale: Data storage saves, organizes, and retrieves data. This gives applications a persistent place to keep information.

options.text: Azure SQL Database is one storage option
options.rationale: Azure SQL Database is listed as an Azure storage option. It is used for mission-critical workloads.

options.text: Azure Cosmos DB supports globally distributed data
options.rationale: Azure Cosmos DB is listed for real-time globally distributed data. It is one of the Azure storage choices.

options.text: Storage replaces the need for model inference
options.error_type: confuses persistent data storage with model processing
options.rationale: Storage keeps information for later use. Inference is when a model applies what it learned during training to new input.
options.better_fit: Choose inference when discussing model processing of new inputs.

feedback.intrinsic: The application may store information but still not produce predictions or generated responses from new input.
feedback.instructional: Storage and inference do different jobs. Storage keeps data; inference processes new input with a trained model.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Storage gives applications a persistent place to keep information.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: That would send the team to the wrong place for visual Azure management.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The Azure portal is a centralized web-based user interface. Scripts and commands are used for programmatic resource creation.

payload.statement: Programmatic resource creation can help repeat the same Azure setup across environments.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The team might repeat setup manually and introduce errors between environments.

payload.statement: Azure networking services help AI applications run reliably, privately, and efficiently.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The app plan might miss an important reliability and privacy layer.

payload.prompt: A hospital team is preparing an AI diagnostic tool that analyzes medical images. The operations lead needs one web-based place to create resources, monitor health, manage roles, and review costs. What should the lead use?

options.rationale: The Azure portal is the centralized web-based UI for managing Azure services. It supports creating resources, monitoring health, managing roles, and reviewing costs in one place.

options.error_type: confuses portal management with programmatic resource creation
options.rationale: A script is useful when the team needs repeatable automated setup. It is not the best match for one web-based place to manage resources, health, roles, and costs visually.
options.better_fit: Choose scripts when the team needs to automate the same setup across environments.

feedback.intrinsic: The operations lead may spend extra time looking for dashboards, role settings, and cost views in the wrong place.
feedback.instructional: For broad visual management across Azure services, choose the Azure portal. Use scripts when repeatable setup is the main need.

options.error_type: confuses Azure-wide management with Foundry project work
options.rationale: The Foundry portal is for developing, testing, and operating projects, models, agents, and related assets. It is not the broad Azure management place for costs, roles, monitoring, and all resources.
options.better_fit: Choose the Foundry portal when working with Foundry projects, models, agents, and related assets.

feedback.intrinsic: The lead could miss Azure-wide billing, access, and resource views needed before release.
feedback.instructional: Foundry focuses on model and agent work. The Azure portal is the web-based place for wider Azure management.

options.error_type: confuses management UI with model access endpoint
options.rationale: A model endpoint is an HTTP address that client code calls to use a deployed model. It is not a management interface for resources, monitoring, roles, or costs.
options.better_fit: Choose a model endpoint when an application needs to send prompts to a deployed model.

feedback.intrinsic: The team would not have a place to review resource health, access settings, or spending.
feedback.instructional: Endpoints are for application calls. Azure portal is for managing services and resources through a web UI.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Azure portal is the web-based place for broad Azure management tasks like resources, monitoring, roles, and costs.

payload.prompt: A finance team is deploying a fraud detection system in test and production. A developer must create the same storage account settings in both environments with fewer manual mistakes. Which approach should the developer choose?

options.text: Run a script or Azure CLI command
options.rationale: Programmatic resource creation uses code or scripts instead of portal clicks. This helps repeat setup across environments and reduce manual errors.

options.text: Click each setting in Azure portal
options.error_type: confuses repeatable automation with manual portal setup
options.rationale: Manual portal work can create a resource, but repeated clicking is more likely to vary between environments. The need is consistent test and production setup.
options.better_fit: Choose portal clicks for visual, one-at-a-time resource management.

feedback.intrinsic: Test and production could end up with different storage settings because someone clicked a different option.
feedback.instructional: When the same setup must be repeated, code or scripts make the deployment more consistent than manual clicks.

options.error_type: confuses model testing with resource creation
options.rationale: The Playground is used to write prompts, test model responses, and configure parameters. It does not create the same storage account settings across environments.
options.better_fit: Choose Playground when testing how a deployed model responds.

feedback.intrinsic: The developer could test prompts but still have no repeatable storage deployment for test and production.
feedback.instructional: Prompt testing and resource deployment are different jobs. Use scripts or Azure CLI commands for repeatable resource creation.

options.error_type: confuses model configuration with Azure resource deployment
options.rationale: Model parameters affect how a model behaves during testing or use. They do not create storage accounts or repeat Azure resource settings.
options.better_fit: Choose model parameter changes when tuning responses in a model test area.

feedback.intrinsic: The storage accounts may still need to be built by hand, which keeps the risk of manual mistakes.
feedback.instructional: Changing model behavior does not deploy resources. Programmatic creation handles repeated setup through code or scripts.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Scripts or Azure CLI commands make repeated resource setup faster and more consistent.

payload.prompt: A manufacturing manager is launching predictive maintenance for factory equipment. The app must stay protected from unauthorized access and connect reliably in cloud and hybrid environments. Which Azure idea best fits this need?

options.rationale: Azure security and networking support identity, access control, network isolation, firewalls, threat detection, monitoring, and private reliable connectivity. That matches both protection from unauthorized access and dependable cloud or hybrid connections.

options.error_type: confuses broad security and networking with access roles only
options.rationale: RBAC is important because it limits access by role. The scenario also needs networking, isolation, monitoring, and reliable connectivity, so RBAC alone is too narrow.
options.better_fit: Choose RBAC when the decision is specifically about limiting access by role.

feedback.intrinsic: The factory app may have role limits but still lack the broader network protection and reliable connectivity it needs.
feedback.instructional: RBAC is one part of protection. The wider security and networking foundation includes access, isolation, monitoring, firewalls, and connectivity.

options.error_type: confuses broad security and networking with secret storage only
options.rationale: Key Vault protects sensitive values such as keys and connection strings. It does not cover all access, networking, monitoring, and firewall needs by itself.
options.better_fit: Choose Key Vault when the team must store keys, tokens, passwords, or connection strings securely.

feedback.intrinsic: Secrets may be protected, but the app could still be missing network isolation and access planning.
feedback.instructional: Key Vault handles secret storage. A full plan for security and networking covers more than hidden values.

options.error_type: confuses app infrastructure protection with model deployment governance
options.rationale: Deployment types are part of model lifecycle and capacity planning. They are not the broad answer for protecting access and connecting cloud and hybrid environments.
options.better_fit: Choose deployment choices when planning model capacity or lifecycle in Foundry.

feedback.intrinsic: The team could make a deployment choice while leaving access and connectivity needs unresolved.
feedback.instructional: Model deployment planning does not replace security and networking. The scenario asks for protection and reliable connections.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The broad need is security plus networking, not just one access or secret feature.

payload.prompt: An education team is building an intelligent tutoring system. The product manager wants only approved teachers, services, and apps to access model deployments and student data. What should the team use?

options.rationale: Microsoft Entra ID helps control who can access resources. RBAC, meaning role-based access control, limits access to model deployments, resources, and data based on assigned roles.

options.error_type: confuses role-based access with secret storage
options.rationale: Key Vault stores sensitive values such as keys and connection strings. It does not define approved teacher and service roles for access by itself.
options.better_fit: Choose Key Vault when the team needs to protect sensitive values used by an application.

feedback.intrinsic: The team may protect keys but still not clearly limit which teachers or services can reach student data.
feedback.instructional: Use Entra ID and RBAC for identity and role-based access. Use Key Vault for sensitive values that must stay hidden.

options.error_type: confuses access control with data storage
options.rationale: Cosmos DB is a storage option for real-time globally distributed data. The scenario is about who may access deployments and student data, not where data is stored.
options.better_fit: Choose Cosmos DB when the application needs real-time globally distributed persistent data.

feedback.intrinsic: The team could pick a storage service but still lack role limits for approved people and services.
feedback.instructional: Storage and access control solve different needs. Entra ID and RBAC are the match for controlling access by role.

options.error_type: confuses access control with web app hosting
options.rationale: App Service hosts web apps, APIs, and background jobs. Hosting does not answer the need to limit access to approved teachers, services, and apps.
options.better_fit: Choose App Service when the team needs to host a web app or API without managing servers.

feedback.intrinsic: The tutoring application may be hosted, but access to model deployments and student data may still be too broad.
feedback.instructional: Hosting decides where an application runs. Entra ID and RBAC decide who and what can access protected resources.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Entra ID and RBAC are the right match for deciding who and what can access resources.

payload.prompt: A developer is building an AI chatbot that calls a model endpoint. The app needs an API key at runtime, but the key must not be placed in code or GitHub. What should the developer do?

options.text: Store it in Azure Key Vault
options.rationale: An API key is a secret because it grants access when calling an endpoint. Azure Key Vault stores secrets instead of placing them in code or GitHub.

options.text: Put it in the source code
options.error_type: confuses hidden secret storage with embedded credentials
options.rationale: Source code should contain application logic, not hidden access values. Putting a key in code exposes the secret instead of protecting it.
options.better_fit: Use source code for the application logic that sends requests and handles responses.

feedback.intrinsic: The key could be exposed to people who should not use the endpoint.
feedback.instructional: A key is a secret. Store it in Key Vault and let the application retrieve it securely at runtime.

options.text: Save it in the prompt text
options.error_type: confuses runtime authentication with model input
options.rationale: Prompt text is input sent to a model. It is not a safe place to keep a value used to authenticate endpoint calls.
options.better_fit: Use prompts to ask for model output, not to store credentials.

feedback.intrinsic: The key could be mixed into model input instead of being protected as an access value.
feedback.instructional: Authentication values belong in protected secret storage. Prompts are for user or application input.

options.error_type: confuses secret value with Azure organization label
options.rationale: A resource group name organizes related Azure resources. It is not a secret and cannot authenticate a call to an endpoint.
options.better_fit: Use resource groups to manage related resources together.

feedback.intrinsic: The chatbot would not have the protected key it needs for endpoint authentication.
feedback.instructional: Resource groups organize resources. API keys are secrets and should be stored in Key Vault.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Key Vault is designed to keep secrets such as API keys protected.

payload.prompt: A retail company is adding a recommendation API to its shopping site. The developer wants quick hosting for the web API without managing the underlying servers. Which Azure service fits?

options.rationale: Azure App Service hosts web applications, APIs, and background jobs. It lets teams deploy web apps quickly without managing the underlying servers.

options.error_type: confuses web app hosting with secret storage
options.rationale: Key Vault protects secrets such as keys, passwords, tokens, and connection strings. It does not host a web API.
options.better_fit: Choose Key Vault to store API keys, passwords, tokens, and connection strings.

feedback.intrinsic: The recommendation API still would not have a place to run for shoppers.
feedback.instructional: Key Vault protects sensitive values. App Service is the hosting choice for web apps and APIs.

options.error_type: confuses hosting with identity access control
options.rationale: Entra ID helps control who and what can access resources. It is not the hosting service that runs a web API.
options.better_fit: Choose Entra ID when deciding who or what can access resources.

feedback.intrinsic: Access may be planned, but the recommendation API still needs a host to run on.
feedback.instructional: Identity and hosting are separate concerns. Entra ID controls access; App Service hosts web apps and APIs.

options.error_type: confuses app hosting with cost management
options.rationale: Billing views help review costs and spending patterns. They do not provide an environment for running a web API.
options.better_fit: Choose billing views when reviewing costs and spending patterns.

feedback.intrinsic: The team could see spending information but still not have the API deployed.
feedback.instructional: Cost review is a management activity. Hosting the API calls for Azure App Service.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Azure App Service is the hosting service for web apps, APIs, and background jobs.

payload.prompt: A finance operations team must redeploy the same fraud detection resources every week for test and production. They can click through the setup each time or create it once with scripts. Which choice better supports consistent deployments?

options.rationale: Programmatic setup uses code or scripts to create resources. It is better for repeated deployments across environments because it makes the same setup easier to reproduce.

options.text: Use the portal manually each time
options.error_type: confuses repeatable deployment with manual management
options.rationale: Manual portal work is useful for visual management. Repeating the same setup by clicking each week can introduce differences between test and production.
options.better_fit: Choose manual portal work for one-off visual resource management tasks.

feedback.intrinsic: Weekly redeployments may drift, with test and production no longer matching.
feedback.instructional: For repeated setup, scripts give a consistent path. Portal management is useful, but it is less suited to frequent identical deployments.

options.error_type: confuses model experimentation with resource automation
options.rationale: The Playground is for testing prompts, model responses, and parameters. It does not automate Azure resource deployments.
options.better_fit: Choose Playground when evaluating a model response before adding it to an application.

feedback.intrinsic: The team may learn how the model responds but still recreate resources by hand every week.
feedback.instructional: Prompt testing is separate from deployment automation. Scripts are the better match for consistent resource creation.

options.error_type: confuses deployment automation with persistent storage
options.rationale: A database can store outputs, logs, state, and other data. It does not make resource deployments consistent by itself.
options.better_fit: Choose storage when the application needs to save outputs, logs, state, or other data.

feedback.intrinsic: Stored results may be available, but the weekly resource setup may still vary.
feedback.instructional: Storage preserves data. Programmatic creation makes repeated deployments consistent.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. For repeated setup across environments, scripts are the stronger choice.

payload.prompt: A manufacturing AI app that predicts machine failures gets heavy request traffic during shift changes. The architect compares adding more running copies with giving one copy more CPU and memory. What concept is being compared?

options.rationale: Scale out, or horizontal scaling, adds more instances. Scale up, or vertical scaling, increases CPU or memory on an existing instance.

options.error_type: confuses scaling choices with Azure organization levels
options.rationale: Tenants and subscriptions organize identity, billing, quotas, and access boundaries. They do not describe adding instances or increasing CPU and memory.
options.better_fit: Choose tenant and subscription when discussing Azure organization and billing boundaries.

feedback.intrinsic: The architect may focus on account organization instead of handling shift-change traffic.
feedback.instructional: Scaling is about compute capacity. Tenants and subscriptions are about organization, billing, and access boundaries.

options.error_type: confuses compute scaling with authentication values
options.rationale: Secrets and keys are sensitive values used for access and authentication. They are not methods for changing compute capacity.
options.better_fit: Choose secrets and keys when securing endpoint calls or connection strings.

feedback.intrinsic: The team may protect access values but still not address the traffic spike.
feedback.instructional: Keys authenticate requests. Scaling adjusts how much compute the application can use.

options.error_type: confuses scaling choices with REST request parts
options.rationale: Headers and body are parts of REST requests. They do not describe adding instances or increasing CPU and memory.
options.better_fit: Choose headers and body when describing how an application sends data to an endpoint.

feedback.intrinsic: The request format may be understood, but the capacity problem remains unsolved.
feedback.instructional: REST request parts describe communication. Scale out and scale up describe compute capacity choices.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The architect is comparing horizontal scaling with vertical scaling.

payload.prompt: A healthcare IT lead is launching an AI tool that analyzes X-rays. Before release, the lead needs to choose tasks that belong in Azure portal management. Which tasks fit?

options.rationale: The Azure portal can monitor usage, performance, and health. This helps the lead track how resources are doing before release.
The Azure portal can manage identities, roles, and access policies. That fits the need to control who can access resources.
The Azure portal can show billing, costs, and spending patterns. That makes it part of broad Azure management.

options.error_type: confuses portal management with model prompting
options.rationale: Prompts are inputs sent to models. They do not replace scripts or Azure portal management tasks.
options.better_fit: Choose prompts when interacting with a model in a client application or Playground.

feedback.intrinsic: The lead may skip real management work such as monitoring, access review, and cost review.
feedback.instructional: Portal management covers resources, monitoring, roles, and costs. Prompts are for model interaction, not Azure management.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. These are Azure portal management tasks: monitoring, access management, and cost review.

payload.prompt: A security analyst reviews a chatbot before production. The analyst finds API keys, tokens, and a database connection string must be protected. Which actions match secrets, keys, and Key Vault?

options.text: Store API keys in Azure Key Vault
options.rationale: API keys are secrets because they grant access. Azure Key Vault stores secrets instead of putting them in code or GitHub.

options.text: Retrieve secrets at runtime using managed identity
options.rationale: Managed identity lets an application retrieve a secret at runtime securely. This avoids embedding credentials in code.
Database connection strings are sensitive values because they can grant access. They should be treated as secrets and protected.

options.text: Grant roles to every user by default
options.error_type: confuses secret handling with broad RBAC access
options.rationale: Granting roles is an access-control decision, not secret storage. Giving roles to every user also does not match the idea of limiting access based on roles.
options.better_fit: Choose RBAC to limit access based on roles, not to store secret values.

feedback.intrinsic: Too many people may gain access while the keys, tokens, and connection string still need protected storage.
feedback.instructional: Secrets belong in Key Vault and can be retrieved securely at runtime. RBAC is for limiting access by role.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Key Vault protects sensitive values, and managed identity helps the app retrieve them securely.

payload.prompt: A factory is connecting a predictive maintenance AI app to cloud resources and some existing systems. The project lead must choose security and networking needs for the plan. Which needs belong?

options.rationale: Identity and access control help ensure only the right people and services can access resources. This is part of Azure's security foundation.
Network isolation and firewalls help protect applications and connections. They support private and reliable communication across cloud and hybrid environments.
Threat detection and monitoring help protect applications and watch their health. They are included in Azure security capabilities.

options.error_type: confuses infrastructure protection with model experimentation
options.rationale: Prompt parameter tuning affects model behavior during experimentation. It does not provide identity controls, network isolation, firewalls, threat detection, or monitoring.
options.better_fit: Choose parameter tuning when experimenting with model behavior in Playground.

feedback.intrinsic: The factory plan may improve model behavior but leave access and network protection incomplete.
feedback.instructional: Security and networking cover identity, access, isolation, firewalls, monitoring, and reliable connectivity. Parameter tuning is a separate model-testing activity.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. These choices protect access, network communication, and app health.

payload.prompt: A retail recommendation app must save information so it can operate, improve, and be monitored later. The data architect is choosing persistent data to store. Which items are valid AI app data?

options.rationale: Training data teaches models patterns. It is one of the data types that applications may need to store.
Logs and telemetry support monitoring and optimization. They are valid persistent data for later review.
Application state supports user-specific continuity. Storing it helps the application keep needed information over time.

options.error_type: confuses persistent AI app data with user interface styling
options.rationale: A button color is interface styling. It is not one of the listed data types used to learn, operate, improve, monitor, or secure the application.
options.better_fit: Choose storage for data such as inputs, outputs, state, configuration, logs, telemetry, and security data.

feedback.intrinsic: The data plan may overlook important operational data while focusing on a visual detail.
feedback.instructional: Persistent storage is for information the application needs later, such as training data, state, logs, telemetry, and configuration.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Applications may store training data, logs, telemetry, state, and other operational data.
